description: #3927 — BRANCH differential over `search_blocks`'s four reachable dispatch arms in `fts::search_with_toggles` (`agaric-store/src/fts/toggle_filter.rs`), plus `run_advanced_query`'s full-text arm, which needs the same materializer-populated `fts_blocks` rows. `search_blocks` had ONE query step (`search_zebrafish`), which leaves every toggle at its `serde(default) = false` and a blank `filter`, so it drove the FTS5 MATCH arm alone while the ratchet read the command as covered. The three other reachable arms differ in FROM clause, ORDER BY and pagination, and the mock had implemented NONE of them. Every block's content arrives via `edit_block` rather than the seed insert: the seed bypasses the materializer, so only an op-driven content write populates `fts_blocks` — a step searching seeded text would compare an empty backend result against a populated mock one. The four `search_blocks` steps share one query family (`widget` / `note`) so each falsifies the others: the same term returns a different row set per arm. #3938 / #3943 extend it: S7 carries markup that HIDES its search term from raw content (the only input on which arm 4 and its post-filter fallthrough disagree, so the `!toggles.any()` branch is falsifiable at last), and S8/S9 are a byte-identical pair used to pin a two-page FTS walk through the `(rank, id)` cursor arm 4 now mints.
name: query_search_blocks_modes

queries.comment: Arm 4 — every toggle off, so `search_with_toggles` short-circuits to the FTS5 MATCH path. The trigram tokenizer matches `widget` as a SUBSTRING and case-insensitively, so all four edited blocks hit. This is the contrast row-set the two post-filter steps below narrow: same term, three different answers.
queries.name: search_fts_widget

queries.comment: Arm 2 — a BLANK query with at least one structural filter is NOT the empty early return: it degrades to `fts_fetch_filter_only_page`, a `FROM blocks b` scan with no FTS5 at all, ordered `b.id DESC`. `ordered` because that recency order is the arm's whole point and the ids are seed ids (byte-identical on both stacks). Pins three things at once: that a blank query with a filter returns rows, that `parentId` restricts to S1's three children (S6 hangs off the other page, S1/S5 are pages), and the DESC direction.
queries.name: search_blank_query_parent_filter

queries.comment: Arm 1 (#3937) — the OTHER half of the blank-query test, and the reason `search_with_toggles` splits its early return in two: with no structural filter at all (`scope` is not a user filter, so `has_filters` is false) the arm returns the EMPTY page by construction, without reading a row. `expect_empty` because that emptiness IS the behaviour, not a selection that happened to miss: it is the negative half of a pair with `search_blank_query_parent_filter` directly above, which is the SAME blank query plus one `parentId` — so the two steps differ in exactly the discriminator (`has_filters`) and a mock that ignored it would redden one of them whichever way it guessed. A mock that answered a blank unfiltered search with the whole database — the natural "no filters means no restriction" reading — fails this step.
queries.name: search_blank_query_unfiltered

queries.comment: Arm 3 — `isRegex` BYPASSES FTS5 entirely and runs the compiled pattern against RAW `blocks.content` over a recency-ordered pre-filtered scan (`ORDER BY b.id DESC`, `next_cursor` always None). The `^` anchor is what makes this un-fakeable by a substring matcher: S4 contains `widget` mid-string and must NOT match, while a literal-substring search for the string `^widget` matches nothing at all. The default `case_sensitive: false` composes an `(?i)` prefix, so the lowercase pattern must still match `Widget`.
queries.name: search_regex_anchored_widget

queries.comment: Arm 5 — `caseSensitive` (with `isRegex` off) takes the post-filter path: the FTS5 trigram candidate set is case-INsensitive, so the arm's job is to narrow it with a `(?-i)` regex over the row's content. Unordered because the survivors keep FTS rank order, which is not comparable across stacks. Falsified by a case-folding implementation, which returns the full `search_fts_widget` set.
queries.name: search_case_sensitive_widget

queries.comment: Arm 5's other toggle — `wholeWord` composes `(?-u:\b)note(?-u:\b)`, so only the block carrying `note` as a standalone word survives; the three carrying `notes` are candidates from FTS and must be dropped by the post-filter. A substring implementation returns all four.
queries.name: search_whole_word_note

queries.comment: `run_advanced_query`'s full-text arm: `fulltext` flips the engine's FROM from `blocks b` to `fts_blocks fts JOIN blocks b`, prefixes the predicate with `fts_blocks MATCH ?1`, shifts every bind by one, and defaults the sort to relevance. Unordered because bm25 rank is not comparable across stacks; the row SET is, and it is what an ignored `fulltext` would blow open — a structural-only query over this space returns all six blocks.
queries.name: advanced_fulltext_widget

queries.comment: #3938 — arm 4's FALSIFIER. `fts_blocks.stripped` is `strip_for_fts_with_maps`'s output, so S7's `Sprocket **gad**get inventory` is indexed as `Sprocket gadget inventory` and the term `gadget` exists ONLY there — it is absent from the raw `blocks.content` column. That is the one input on which the `!toggles.any()` fast path and its post-filter fallthrough disagree: `compose_literal_pattern` composes `(?i)gadget` and `post_filter_row` runs it against RAW content, which does not match. Delete the fast path (on either stack) and this step returns []. Before #3938 the mock folded over raw content, so it could not express the difference and the arm was declared covered-but-not-falsifiable.
queries.name: search_fts_stripped_markup

queries.comment: #3943 — page 1 of a PAGED FTS search. S8 and S9 carry byte-identical content, so they rank identically on both stacks (bm25 depends on term frequency and document length, both equal) and `ORDER BY fts.rank, b.id` is decided by the id tiebreak alone — the one shape in which an FTS page is comparable across stacks at all, since the rank VALUES are not. `ordered` for that reason. Records `has_more: true` WITH a `v1:{id,rank}` cursor: the mock used to answer `has_more: true` with `next_cursor: null` here, which no backend produces and no client can act on.
queries.name: search_fts_paged_page1

queries.comment: #3943 — page 2, resumed from page 1's `(rank, id)` cursor. This is the step a `next_cursor: null` regression reddens: the mock would re-deliver B8 forever. Each stack feeds itself its OWN cursor bytes, so what is compared is the ROW the resumed page holds.
queries.name: search_fts_paged_page2
